text: This lesson covers PL-SQL packages, and it's one of the most important concepts in this whole chapter, because it's a concept T-SQL genuinely doesn't have. A package groups related procedures, functions, variables, cursors, and types into one named unit, split into two pieces: a specification and a body.

The specification is the public interface. Here, order package exposes one function and one procedure, plus a public variable. Anything listed in the spec is callable from outside the package — callers write order package dot get order total, and never need to know how it's actually implemented.

The body holds the real code. Every routine from the spec gets its full implementation here — but the body can also contain entirely private helpers, like compute tax here, that never appear in the spec and so can never be called from outside the package. And here's the real payoff: you can rewrite the body and recompile only the body. Callers, and the spec itself, stay completely untouched.

Now the genuinely unique part. A package-level variable like g last order checked is initialized once per session, and then keeps its value for the rest of that session, across many separate calls, with no cleanup step required. It behaves like a small piece of session-scoped state living inside the package itself.

T-SQL has nothing that maps onto this one to one. The closest it gets is grouping related procedures in the same schema — an organizational convention, not a language feature. No spec and body split, no private package state, and critically, no built-in way for a group of procedures to share a variable that automatically persists for the life of a session.

Next lesson: anonymous blocks and DBMS output — running PL-SQL ad hoc without wrapping it in a procedure, and the one setting you need to flip before you'll actually see any printed output. See you there.
